output.title: What churn signals hide before the customer leaves
output.body:
Most churn does not arrive as a dramatic cancellation. It usually hides in quieter signals: fewer orders, longer gaps between purchases, repeated support questions, or customers who stop using one part of the service and keep paying out of habit. The job is not to chase every wobble. It is to separate active signals from passive erosion.

Active signals are the obvious ones: a cancellation notice, a payment problem, a sharp complaint. Those need a human decision now. Passive signals are slower and easier to miss. For an online shop, an illustrative example is a customer who used to buy every week and then goes three weeks with no order. That is not proof of churn, but it is a warning worth looking at.

The bounded workflow decision is simple: decide which signals you can already see in a spreadsheet, CRM, or support inbox, and which ones stay invisible until it is too late. If the data exists, a small workflow can flag the pattern and route it to manual review. It should not decide the response on its own. Human approval stays in charge.

A practical next step is manual: pull the last 12 months of order history, support tickets, login activity, and payment records, then pick two or three customers who left or went quiet. Write down the first signal you could have seen at the time. That audit will show whether you have a workflow gap or just a feeling wearing a trench coat.
